lines.speaker: q
lines.text: Can measles really erase my immune memory?

lines.speaker: a
lines.text: Yes. Measles doesn't just give you a rash and a fever. It slips into the cells that remember your old infections and wipes many of them out, so germs you already beat can come back.

lines.speaker: a
lines.text: And the timing matters. On November 17, 2026, the Pan American Health Organization announced that the United States had lost its measles elimination status, held since 2000.

lines.speaker: a
lines.text: That happens when one chain of measles keeps spreading for a full year. By mid-November, the CDC had counted 5,412 cases in 2026, and states had reported 10 deaths.

lines.speaker: a
lines.text: Canada lost the same status a year earlier, in November 2025. Measles is settling back into North America, one unvaccinated classroom at a time.

lines.speaker: q
lines.text: So what does measles actually do?

lines.speaker: a
lines.text: Let's start with the illness itself, then follow the virus into your immune system's memory bank.

lines.speaker: q
lines.text: What happens when you catch measles?

lines.speaker: a
lines.text: First comes a high fever, a cough, a runny nose and red, watery eyes. It looks like a bad cold.

lines.speaker: a
lines.text: Two or three days later, tiny white spots appear inside the cheeks, like grains of salt on red skin. Doctors call them Koplik spots, and they're a giveaway for measles.

lines.speaker: a
lines.text: Then the rash erupts. Flat red blotches start at the hairline and spread down the face, the neck, the chest, all the way to the feet.

lines.speaker: a
lines.text: About one in five unvaccinated Americans who catch measles ends up in the hospital.

lines.speaker: q
lines.text: Is it usually just a rash?

lines.speaker: a
lines.text: Not always. Up to one in twenty children with measles gets pneumonia, as the lungs fill with fluid. That's the most common way measles kills young children.

lines.speaker: a
lines.text: Overall, about one to three of every thousand children who catch it die from lung or brain complications.

lines.speaker: a
lines.text: In about one in a thousand cases, the virus inflames the brain. That's encephalitis, and it can leave a child deaf or with lasting brain damage.

lines.speaker: a
lines.text: And rarely, the virus hides in the brain for years. Seven to ten years later, it wakes up as SSPE, a slow brain disease that is always fatal.

lines.speaker: q
lines.text: Why does measles spread so easily?

lines.speaker: a
lines.text: Because it floats. A cough sprays tiny droplets into the air, and they hang there like invisible smoke.

lines.speaker: a
lines.text: Measles can stay in a room's air for up to two hours after the sick person has left. You can walk in later and breathe it in.

lines.speaker: a
lines.text: Worse, people spread it for four days before the rash appears, while they still think it's just a cold, and for four days after.

lines.speaker: a
lines.text: If ten unprotected people share a room with someone who has measles, up to nine of them will catch it.

lines.speaker: q
lines.text: How does that compare to other viruses?

lines.speaker: a
lines.text: Scientists use a number called R naught: how many people one case infects in a crowd with no immunity. For measles, it's often quoted at twelve to eighteen.

lines.speaker: a
lines.text: For the seasonal flu, it's only about one and a quarter. That's why measles is the first disease to come back when vaccination rates slip.

lines.speaker: q
lines.text: How does measles reach my immune memory?

lines.speaker: a
lines.text: Your immune memory lives in white blood cells called memory B cells and memory T cells. Each one carries a record of a germ you've met or been vaccinated against.

lines.speaker: a
lines.text: Measles carries a key that fits a lock on their surface, a receptor called CD150. Memory T cells carry more of these locks than fresh, untrained ones.

lines.speaker: a
lines.text: So the virus heads straight for them. It unlocks the memory cells, moves in, copies itself, and the infected cells are destroyed.

lines.speaker: q
lines.text: Doesn't the body just replace them?

lines.speaker: a
lines.text: It replaces the numbers, not the records. New white blood cells flood in to fight measles, so blood counts look normal again within weeks.

lines.speaker: a
lines.text: But many of those new cells only know measles. The old cells that remembered your past colds, flu and other infections are gone.

lines.speaker: a
lines.text: It's like a library fire. The shelves get restocked fast, but with copies of one book, while the rare volumes you collected are ash.

lines.speaker: q
lines.text: How do we know memory really gets erased?

lines.speaker: a
lines.text: Surprisingly, the best evidence came from an outbreak. In 2019, a team led by Michael Mina at Harvard tested blood from 77 unvaccinated children in the Netherlands, before and after they caught measles.

lines.speaker: a
lines.text: They used a tool called VirScan. It dips a drop of blood into thousands of tiny virus fragments and reads which ones your antibodies grab.

lines.speaker: a
lines.text: Two months after measles, the children had lost between eleven and seventy-three percent of their antibodies against other germs.

lines.speaker: q
lines.text: Seventy-three percent? Of everything?

lines.speaker: a
lines.text: Of their antibody variety, in the hardest-hit child. Antibodies against viruses and bacteria they had already beaten, from flu viruses to common bacteria, simply vanished from the blood.

lines.speaker: a
lines.text: Healthy children followed over the same months kept about ninety percent of their antibody variety. So this was not normal forgetting.

lines.speaker: a
lines.text: Children who had a severe case tended to lose more. And in monkeys infected on purpose, roughly half their old antibodies were still missing five months later.

lines.speaker: q
lines.text: Does the immune system ever reset fully?

lines.speaker: a
lines.text: Not quickly. The same year, a team in Britain and the Netherlands, led by Velislava Petrova, read the genes of the B cells in twenty-six unvaccinated Dutch children, before and after measles.

lines.speaker: a
lines.text: Memory B cells built up against old infections had disappeared from the blood. And the fresh B cells that replaced them were immature, like a newborn's.

lines.speaker: a
lines.text: The researchers called it a more baby-like immune system. Their defenses looked less experienced, closer to an infant's than a school kid's.

lines.speaker: a
lines.text: Some children show signs of a weakened immune system for up to five years, even when their white blood cell counts look perfectly normal.

lines.speaker: q
lines.text: Does that actually make people sicker?

lines.speaker: a
lines.text: In ferrets, yes. Ferrets vaccinated against flu caught a measles-like virus, their flu antibodies dropped, and when flu hit them, they got sicker.

lines.speaker: q
lines.text: How long does the danger last?

lines.speaker: a
lines.text: About two to three years. In 2015, Mina's team lined up decades of death records from the United States, England and Denmark.

lines.speaker: a
lines.text: Every measles wave was followed, about two to three years later, by a wave of children dying from other infections, the ones measles had left them open to.

lines.speaker: a
lines.text: When the vaccine wiped out measles, those other deaths dropped too. A puzzle that had sat there since the nineteen sixties suddenly made sense.

lines.speaker: a
lines.text: Mina put it simply: if your child gets measles and then pneumonia two years later, you wouldn't tie the two together. But they can be linked.

lines.speaker: q
lines.text: How many deaths are we talking about?

lines.speaker: a
lines.text: Before vaccines, their model suggests measles may have been behind up to half of all childhood deaths from infectious disease in rich countries, mostly through this hidden shadow.

lines.speaker: a
lines.text: Before 1963, the U.S. saw an estimated three to four million measles cases a year, and about four to five hundred deaths from measles itself.

lines.speaker: q
lines.text: Can the vaccine cause the same amnesia?

lines.speaker: a
lines.text: No. Mina's team also tested children before and after their first MMR shot. Their antibody libraries stayed intact.

lines.speaker: a
lines.text: The vaccine virus is weakened. It trains your immune system to recognize measles without wiping out the antibody library you already have.

lines.speaker: a
lines.text: Two doses of MMR are about ninety-seven percent effective at stopping measles. One dose, about ninety-three.

lines.speaker: a
lines.text: Kids get the first dose at twelve to fifteen months, and the second between four and six years old.

lines.speaker: q
lines.text: So why are cases rising again?

lines.speaker: a
lines.text: Because fewer kids are getting the shots. Kindergarten MMR coverage fell from ninety-five percent in 2019 to about ninety-two percent now.

lines.speaker: a
lines.text: That sounds small, but it leaves almost three hundred thousand kindergartners unprotected each year. And measles needs about ninety-five percent coverage to be kept out.

lines.speaker: a
lines.text: Exemptions keep hitting new records, and outbreaks flare wherever many kids in one school or town are unvaccinated, then spread outward.

lines.speaker: q
lines.text: Can you get your immune memory back?

lines.speaker: a
lines.text: Partly. Every time a survivor meets an old germ again, the immune system relearns it, cell by cell. But that takes months to years.

lines.speaker: a
lines.text: And until then, old enemies can strike again: another flu, another ear infection, another chest infection, right when defenses are at their weakest.

lines.speaker: a
lines.text: So Mina's team suggested a shortcut. After measles, doctors could consider booster shots of earlier routine vaccines, like polio and hepatitis, to refill the lost shelves.

lines.speaker: q
lines.text: Do adults lose memory too?

lines.speaker: a
lines.text: The big studies were done in children. Adults are less studied, but adults over twenty are more likely to have measles complications, so protection matters at every age.

lines.speaker: q
lines.text: So what should I actually do?

lines.speaker: a
lines.text: Check your vaccine records. If you're not sure you had two MMR doses, ask your doctor about a blood test or an extra dose. And after a measles infection, ask about catching up on routine vaccines.

lines.speaker: a
lines.text: Measles doesn't just make you sick. It erases your immune memory.

lines.speaker: q
lines.text: Subscribe for more of the science inside your body, and tell us in the comments: did you ever have measles, or do you know your vaccine record?
